items.title: TightVNC Pre-Auth RCE Vulnerability Lets Hackers Execute Code on Windows PCs, PoC Released
items.summary: A TightVNC Viewer vulnerability can let attackers execute code on Windows PCs before a password prompt appears. Research credited to SeongJoon Cho of SSD Labs Korea includes proof-of-concept exploit code targeting TightVNC 2.8.88 x64. The attack uses a malicious VNC server to send screen data that corrupts the viewer’s memory. The affected component is the viewer, not simply any Windows machine running a TightVNC server. Attackers need either network access to a viewer in Listening Mode or a user who connects the viewer to an attacker-controlled server. The supplied disclosure does not establish active exploitation. The flaw begins when the server announces its screen size through the Remote Framebuffer protocol (RFB) . TightVNC calculates the memory needed to hold that screen, but converts the result into a 32-bit integer. Large dimensions cause the value to wrap around, leaving a smaller allocation than expected. In the reported example, a server announces a 32,768-by-32,769 screen using 32 bits per pixel. The viewer allocates only 128 KB while retaining dimensions representing more than 4 GB of pixel data. Later screen updates write outside that small buffer because the pointer calculation lacks a check against the allocated size. TightVNC Pre-Auth RCE Vulnerability The PoC turns this memory corruption into code execution. It first changes an outgoing buffer’s length to leak nearby memory, revealing addresses needed to bypass address randomization. It then redirects a function call and uses return-oriented programming, which reuses existing code, to launch a process through Windows’ CreateProcessW function. Listening Mode exposes the viewer on TCP port 5500 and, according to the disclosure, accepts incoming server connections without a password or IP restriction. An attacker who can reach that port can target the viewer directly. An outbound connection to a rogue support server creates another route, with exploitation occurring before authentication. These conditions differ from VNC connection hijacking that relies on weak passwords. They also differ from remote access tools disguised as installers , where users install legitimate software under pretenses. Here, the attack targets memory handling inside the viewer itself. The researchers say the vendor did not respond and patched the issue on October 3, 2026. However, TightVNC’s official release notices identify October 2 and October 5 security updates, so the exact fix date remains unclear. The vendor says versions 2.8.89 and 2.8.90 address Viewer security issues and recommends 2.8.90 for that branch. Administrators should update affected viewers, turn off unnecessary Listening Mode, restrict port 5500 to trusted systems, and avoid untrusted VNC servers. Network restrictions reduce exposure but do not replace patching the vulnerable viewer. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs .

items.title: Hackers Target 61 GitHub Repositories With Command Injection Attacks to Steal CI/CD Secrets
items.summary: Hackers targeted 61 public GitHub repositories in a coordinated command injection campaign designed to steal data from automated development systems. Radware researchers identified 83 malicious issues, pull requests, and comments posted on September 1, 2026, with evidence that injected commands executed inside two GitHub Actions workflows. The findings show how routine project discussions can become entry points into software build systems. According to Radware’s investigation, 77 malicious items appeared within about 43 minutes. Six more followed in a second wave lasting roughly two minutes. Targets included Google LangExtract, Trivy, Brave Browser, MLflow, ToolJet, and PX4-Autopilot. Their inclusion does not mean every project was breached. The attack chain (source: Radware ) The campaign exploited workflows that placed user-controlled text directly into shell scripts. GitHub Actions can automatically respond when someone opens an issue, submits a pull request, or posts a comment. These tasks may check titles, assign labels, or send notifications. Hackers Target 61 GitHub Repositories Attackers placed Bash command substitution expressions, written as $(), inside that content. When a vulnerable workflow inserted the text into executable shell code, Bash treated the embedded expression as a command rather than ordinary text. Wrapping the inserted title in double quotes did not prevent execution. The payload ran env to collect environment variables, encoded the output with Base64, removed newline characters, and used curl to attempt an HTTP POST request. PX4/PX4-Autopilot — Pull Request #28488 (source : Radware ) Every verified payload pointed to 54.205.16[.]142 on port 8443, with a separate collection identifier for each attempt. Despite the port number, the connection used HTTP rather than HTTPS. The risk depended on what each job could access. Environment variables could contain service tokens, deployment credentials, or internal settings. GitHub Actions secrets are not automatically available to every workflow, so execution alone does not establish that sensitive credentials were stolen. Snouzy/workout-cool Issue #251, showing the command-injection payload in the Issue title (source : Radware ) In PX4-Autopilot, a pull request posing as a documentation correction carried the payload in its title. A title-checking workflow inserted that title into a Bash command invoking Python. Logs showed a command-substitution warning and returned content beginning with GIF89a, replacing the malicious expression. In Snouzy/workout-cool, an issue notification workflow inserted the attacker’s title directly into a Bash variable assignment. A warning tied to that line confirmed command substitution. A later Discord request failed because its body contained invalid JSON, although that failure did not prove successful data theft. Radware did not confirm stolen secrets, repository write access, source code changes, or compromised releases. Researchers also found signs that some participating accounts may have been hijacked, including one owner publicly denying opening a malicious issue. The findings complement earlier reporting on GhostAction credential theft and the tj-actions supply chain attack . Those incidents used different routes but also put CI/CD secrets at risk. Account-owner comments denying authorship of the Issue and reporting subsequent account-protection actions (source : Radware) Maintainers should pass untrusted titles through environment variables instead of inserting them into shell source, avoid eval, and limit workflow permissions. Teams finding execution evidence should review available secrets, rotate potentially exposed credentials, inspect audit logs, and investigate unexpected outbound traffic. Keep notification jobs separate from privileged release workflows to reduce the damage an injected command could cause. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs .

items.title: Hackers Drain Bitcoin Hot Wallets on BTCPay Servers, Users Urged to Shut Down Immediately
items.summary: BTCPay Server has issued an urgent warning after receiving reports that attackers were draining Bitcoin hot wallets on its servers. The open-source payment processor told operators to shut down their installations immediately and keep them offline while its team investigates the thefts. The alert raises concerns for merchants holding funds in wallets managed through affected servers. In its November 1 security notice, the project said: “We are receiving reports of hot wallets on BTCPay Servers being swept by unauthorized attackers.” It instructed operators to run ./btcpay-down.sh until the investigation is complete. The warning did not limit that instruction to specific software versions or announce that restarting was safe. We are receiving reports of hot wallets on BTCPay Servers being swept by unauthorized attackers. If you're running an instance, please shut it down (./btcpay-down.sh) until we complete the investigation. — BTCPay Server (@BtcpayServer) November 1, 2026 BTCPay Server Warns Early findings point toward outdated installations. Founder Nicolas Dorier reportedly said affected servers were running versions older than 2.4.2 and that attackers had logged in as administrators. However, investigators had not established how they gained that access, leaving the initial entry point unconfirmed. Dorier also said the project’s public servers running version 2.4.7 had not been attacked. That observation is important, but it does not prove every updated installation is safe. Operators should not treat the absence of reported attacks against those servers as an all-clear while the broader shutdown warning remains in place. The available reports did not provide a confirmed loss total or a count of affected installations. No complete technical account has established whether the attackers used stolen login details, a software flaw, or another route to administrator access. BTCPay Server lets merchants accept Bitcoin directly using self-hosted software. Its wallet documentation explains that an enabled hot wallet signs transactions using a seed stored on the server. This makes payments convenient, but places sensitive signing material inside the online environment. A server breach can therefore put funds at risk, depending on the access obtained. The incident highlights risks also covered in Cyber Security News reporting on fake crypto wallet screens stealing recovery phrases and Google Sheets campaigns that swap wallet addresses . Those campaigns involve different methods, and neither has been linked to the BTCPay thefts. The shared concern is protecting wallet secrets and checking where funds are sent. Recent Patches Do Not Confirm the Cause The warning follows BTCPay Server 2.4.7, released October 29. Its official release notes list 85 security findings addressed after reports from Anthropic’s OSS Scanner program. These included one critical, 13 high, 52 medium, and 19 low-severity findings, covering permissions, authentication, payment handling, and other functions. There is no confirmed link between those fixes and the current wallet drains. A separate earlier advisory for version 2.4.2 concerned exposed Lightning Network Daemon credentials. BTCPay explicitly said its own on-chain wallets, including hot wallets, were not affected by that earlier issue. Combining the two incidents would misstate what developers have confirmed. For now, the clearest official action is to stop the server with ./btcpay-down.sh and leave it offline pending further guidance. Updating alone should not be presented as resolving an active compromise. Operators also need to distinguish confirmed developer instructions from community reports as the investigation develops and the team determines the attack path, affected deployments, and recovery steps.[ x ]

items.title: Inside a successful AWS European Sovereign Cloud exercise to demonstrate independent operation
items.summary: On Saturday, October 24, 2026 we conducted a successful exercise demonstrating that the AWS European Sovereign Cloud can operate without depending on any infrastructure outside the European Union (EU). This was the first public technical exercise demonstrating the independence of a sovereign cloud Region. The AWS European Sovereign Cloud is a new, independent cloud partition for Europe that became generally available in January 2026, with its first AWS Region in Brandenburg, Germany. It is physically and logically separate from other AWS Regions , with no critical dependencies on non-EU infrastructure, and all customer content and customer-created metadata remains in the EU. The AWS European Sovereign Cloud is managed through dedicated European legal entities established under German law and operated entirely within Europe. My fellow Managing Director, Stefan Hoechbauer, and I called for the exercise. We are EU citizens residing in the EU, responsible for its management and operations, including its infrastructure, technology, and services. Only EU residents located in the EU control its operations and support, and AWS is gradually transitioning the AWS European Sovereign Cloud to be operated exclusively by EU citizens located in the EU. What we did In standard operations, the AWS European Sovereign Cloud uses two global systems: the AWS Global Network backbone, and a dedicated system operated by the local EU team to manage limited, controlled transfers of operational AWS data. As we explained ahead of the exercise , neither is critical to running the AWS European Sovereign Cloud. During the exercise, the team switched off both systems, and traffic that normally travels across the AWS Global Network backbone rerouted securely over the public internet. The AWS European Sovereign Cloud can operate independently at any time, and for several hours on October 24 the team showed exactly that, running it on only its own software and hardware resources, operated by EU-resident staff within the EU. Workloads continued running, and customers could still access their data. The exercise did not affect service availability within the AWS European Sovereign Cloud, other AWS Regions, or private connectivity through AWS Direct Connect . When the exercise finished, traffic returned to its normal path. Why we ran it Transparency is at the core of our digital sovereignty commitment, so we ran the AWS European Sovereign Cloud exercise openly and reported back on the outcome. The exercise produced verifiable technical and operational evidence that the AWS European Sovereign Cloud can continue to operate independently within the EU. It turns a design claim into a verified result. Organizations in regulated industries and the public sector can take this result to regulators and their boards as evidence for their compliance and assurance documents. What customers and partners are saying “Digital sovereignty is ultimately about trust and safeguarding business continuity. The successful demonstration of the AWS European Sovereign Cloud’s operational independence is an important proof point for European organizations with the most stringent sovereignty requirements. Combined with Capgemini’s European heritage, presence and AWS capabilities, we can deliver a sovereign proposition in Europe, for Europe, by Europeans, enabling clients to accelerate secure and resilient cloud and AI transformation at scale whilst assuring business continuity.” – Fernando Alvarez, Chief Strategy and Development Officer and Group Executive Board Member, Capgemini “Autonomy, resilience and operational control are foundations driving digital sovereignty concerns across the public sector and regulated industries. Achieving sovereignty requires more than a sound and consistent architecture; it demands operational evidence to build trust. The AWS European Sovereign Cloud team has provided evidence, supporting organizations on the transformation of their critical data and digital assets toward greater sovereign control. Having engaged with this team since the inception of the project, and as a Launch Partner of the AWS Digital Sovereignty Competency, Atos helps customers define their sovereignty roadmaps, adopt the appropriate graduated solutions, and confidently operate and govern their target sovereignty posture.” – Michael Kollar, Digital Sovereignty Leader and Head of Cloud & Modern Infrastructure and Digital Workplace, Atos Group “For organizations in regulated industries, meeting strict data and operational requirements cannot come at the cost of a great customer experience. Running on the AWS European Sovereign Cloud, Genesys can help European organizations deliver exactly that, with their data and operations kept in the EU. Seeing the AWS European Sovereign Cloud operate independently under real conditions helps give our shared customers added confidence to move their most sensitive workloads to the cloud.” – Daniel Karadza, Senior Director, Partners and Alliances, EMEA Central and Benelux, Genesys “Operational independence is a defining pillar of digital sovereignty, and the AWS European Sovereign Cloud has shown what that means in practice. It runs without reliance on any infrastructure outside the EU and is operated entirely by EU residents, which makes it a strong fit for Europe’s regulated industries and public sector. As an early collaborator with the AWS European Sovereign Cloud team before its launch, Accenture is uniquely positioned to help clients navigate sovereignty requirements and scale with greater confidence and control.” – Emanuele Baldassarre, Managing Director, Accenture Learn more To learn more about the design and digital sovereignty controls of the AWS European Sovereign Cloud, visit aws.eu . If you have questions about this exercise or want to discuss your workloads, reach out to AWS Support or contact your AWS Account team. Stéphane Israël Stéphane is the leader and Managing Director of the AWS European Sovereign Cloud. He is responsible for the management and operations of the AWS European Sovereign Cloud, including infrastructure, technology, and services, in addition to broader digital sovereignty efforts at AWS. Prior to AWS, he was the CEO of Arianespace, where he oversaw numerous successful space missions, including the launch of the James Webb Space Telescope.

items.title: Critical Certificate Validation Flaw in LXD and Incus Could Give Hackers Control of Linux Hosts
items.summary: A critical certificate validation flaw in LXD and Incus could let remote attackers bypass login checks and take control of clusters and managed virtual machines. The weakness affects the HTTPS management listener, placing exposed Linux systems at risk without requiring a password, stolen private key, or user interaction. Incus rates its flaw critical, with a CVSS score of 10.0. The Incus security advisory , published on October 29, says the bug has existed since the project’s initial release. Canonical published its related LXD record, CVE-2026-112816, on October 30. Although Ubuntu assigns that record Medium priority, it describes an unauthenticated path to full cluster and virtual machine access. Certificate Validation Flaw in LXD and Incus The problem lies in how the service checks certificates presented during an HTTPS connection. The TLS handshake proves that a client holds the private key for the first certificate it submits. However, the remaining certificates in that chain are controlled by the client and are not verified. Authentication checks then compare every certificate in the submitted chain against the server’s trust store. This creates a gap between proving ownership of a certificate and accepting its identity. An attacker can append a trusted certificate’s public part to their own chain and be accepted as its owner, despite lacking the matching private key. Public certificates are not secrets. Servers return their certificates during TLS handshakes, meaning an attacker needs no existing account to obtain one. According to the advisory, presenting the server’s own certificate grants database gateway access, while presenting another cluster member’s certificate grants internal cluster access and bypasses authorization entirely. This differs from the container escape flaws covered in Cyber Security News’ runc vulnerability report . Rather than breaking out of an isolated workload, this bug targets the trusted management layer that controls access to the environment. The Incus advisory says attackers can impersonate trusted client, metrics, or server certificates when they have the relevant public certificate. The same weakness allows renewal or deletion of trust store entries through self-service paths. It also affects authentication for the agent connection between hosts and virtual machines. Another affected area is the authorization scriptlet, a script used to make access decisions. Incus passed the unverified certificate chain to this script, allowing attacker-chosen certificates to influence its decisions. This also affects connections using tokens or OpenID Connect, because those clients can still present certificates during the handshake. Fixed Versions and Immediate Protection Incus lists versions before 7.6.0 as affected and version 7.6.0 onward as patched. Canonical’s LXD notice identifies fixes in versions 4.0.15, 5.0.11, 5.21.9, and 6.10.1 for the affected release branches. Administrators should check their installed version against the relevant vendor advisory. Until updates are applied, Incus advises restricting HTTPS listener access to trusted hosts. There is no configuration-based workaround that fixes the underlying validation error. Network restrictions reduce exposure but do not replace patching. Cyber Security News’ Linux container security guide provides broader context on protecting container environments. For this flaw, the immediate focus is narrower: update affected services and limit who can reach their management interfaces. Neither cited advisory reports active exploitation, so exposure should not be confused with confirmed compromise. AI is making cyberattacks faster and cheaper. Are your defenses ready to respond at machine speed?

Certificate Validation Flaw in LXD and Incus

The problem lies in how the service checks certificates presented during an HTTPS connection. The TLS handshake proves that a client holds the private key for the first certificate it submits. However, the remaining certificates in that chain are controlled by the client and are not verified.

Authentication checks then compare every certificate in the submitted chain against the server’s trust store. This creates a gap between proving ownership of a certificate and accepting its identity. An attacker can append a trusted certificate’s public part to their own chain and be accepted as its owner, despite lacking the matching private key.

Public certificates are not secrets. Servers return their certificates during TLS handshakes, meaning an attacker needs no existing account to obtain one. According to the advisory, presenting the server’s own certificate grants database gateway access, while presenting another cluster member’s certificate grants internal cluster access and bypasses authorization entirely.

This differs from the container escape flaws covered in Cyber Security News’ runc vulnerability report. Rather than breaking out of an isolated workload, this bug targets the trusted management layer that controls access to the environment.

The Incus advisory says attackers can impersonate trusted client, metrics, or server certificates when they have the relevant public certificate. The same weakness allows renewal or deletion of trust store entries through self-service paths. It also affects authentication for the agent connection between hosts and virtual machines.

Another affected area is the authorization scriptlet, a script used to make access decisions. Incus passed the unverified certificate chain to this script, allowing attacker-chosen certificates to influence its decisions. This also affects connections using tokens or OpenID Connect, because those clients can still present certificates during the handshake.

Fixed Versions and Immediate Protection

Incus lists versions before 7.6.0 as affected and version 7.6.0 onward as patched. Canonical’s LXD notice identifies fixes in versions 4.0.15, 5.0.11, 5.21.9, and 6.10.1 for the affected release branches. Administrators should check their installed version against the relevant vendor advisory.

Until updates are applied, Incus advises restricting HTTPS listener access to trusted hosts. There is no configuration-based workaround that fixes the underlying validation error. Network restrictions reduce exposure but do not replace patching.

Cyber Security News’ Linux container security guide provides broader context on protecting container environments. For this flaw, the immediate focus is narrower: update affected services and limit who can reach their management interfaces. Neither cited advisory reports active exploitation, so exposure should not be confused with confirmed compromise.
